fetched_contents.text: Summary of evidence - Guideline: Optimal Serum and Red Blood Cell Folate Concentrations in Women of Reproductive Age for Prevention of Neural Tube Defects The methodological approach agreed by members of the guideline development group entailed a combination of narrative reviews, data analysis and modelling, as well as systematic reviews following the procedures of the Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions (38). A summary of the evidence and the findings follows, and full details may be found in the references cited. Genetic, biological and sociodemographic determinants of folate status (serum, plasma or red blood cell folate) in women of reproductive age The evidence to address this question was gathered from several narrative and systematic reviews: * two narrative reviews that identified and broadly assessed the determinants of folate status and narrowed down the factors that were more likely to affect the establishment of folate thresholds (39, 40); these therefore needed an in-depth systematic assessment; * a systematic review and meta-analysis of trials and observational studies assessing the association between the MTHFR 677C→T polymorphism and blood folate concentrations (41); * an analysis of the global distribution of genotypic frequencies of eight polymorphisms in genes of the folate/homocysteine metabolic pathway in various populations (42); * two narrative reviews on the interactions between folate and folate-dependent drugs used in malaria prevention (26, 27). Multiple factors influence folate status, including the MTHFR 677C→T gene polymorphism, physiological status (age, pregnancy/lactation), and contextual factors such as comorbidity and low socioeconomic status. A narrative review (39) summarized the history of folate as a public health issue, and its biology, as well as specific considerations for the use and interpretation of folate biomarkers across a range of clinical and population-based uses. Folate status, measured through serum folate or red blood cell folate, is altered in disease. In the clinical setting, the primary aim is to diagnose folate deficiency, and serum folate is a useful marker of folate status in this setting, although it may be variable, with concentrations influenced by recent consumption of a high-folate meal, daily or intermittent folic acid supplements, and medications. Repeated measures over time can make serum folate testing more informative. Red blood cell folate is reflective of long-term status, so may reflect status prior to disease. Increased folate requirements may be present when there are increased physiological requirements (e.g. pregnancy, lactation), pathological conditions (e.g. malignancy, inflammatory conditions, certain anaemias), or drug use (e.g. anticonvulsants, methotrexate, sulfasalazine). Decreased folate availability may occur when there is impaired folate absorption (e.g. alcohol consumption, coeliac disease) or reduced dietary intake (e.g. low intake of folic acid-fortified foods, dark green leafy vegetables, legumes, selected fruit such as orange juice) (43). In conclusion, the main determinants of folate status are intake, use of antifolate medications and genetic background, including the gene polymorphism MTHFR 677C→T. Genetic variation has a role in folate metabolism but the impact of a particular variant on the risk of diseases is difficult to establish, owing to the presence of many confounders in the relevant studies (41). Both genetic and non-genetic variation in the population have to be considered when evaluating polymorphisms. This may be particularly relevant when studying a folate-related variant involved in health outcomes that are also associated with other nutrients, in addition to folate. The systematic review included 40 controlled trials and observational studies that reported serum, plasma, or red blood cell folate concentrations and MTHFR C677→T (rs1801133) genotype in healthy women (41). The meta-analysis (41) allowed estimation of percentage differences in blood folate concentrations between MTHFR C677T genotypes. Six studies that utilized the microbiological assay to measure serum/plasma and red blood cell concentrations showed a clear pattern of CC<CT<TT A greater difference was found for CC>TT (serum/plasma 13%; red blood cell 8%), CT>TT (serum plasma 7%; red blood cell 8%) and CT>TT (serum/plasma 6%; red blood cell 9%). A reverse pattern was revealed by the results of the meta-analysis of the studies that utilized protein-binding assays for measuring red blood cell folate concentrations. Another review (42) analysed the genotypic frequencies of eight polymorphisms in genes of the folate/homocysteine metabolic pathway, in 1350 Mestizo and American-Indian subjects from different regions in Mexico and 836 individuals from European, African and Asian populations of the 1000 Genomes Project. In Mexican Mestizo individuals, the prevalence of the MTHFR C677T risk genotype (TT) was 25%, while in American-Indian populations the prevalence was 57%. Altogether, risk genotypes showed regional differences in Mexico, illustrating differential geographical distribution of the risk variants in the folate/homocysteine metabolic pathway relative to ethnic background. These data suggest that needs for folic acid and vitamin B supplementation may be increased in some regions of the world. The association between the MTHFR C677T genotype and NTD has been investigated, with controversial results. Findings of recent systematic reviews and meta-analyses (44) have suggested that maternal MTHFR C677T genotype is a risk factor for NTD, and the strength of this association may vary across geographic regions, probably owing to differences in genetic background and environmental factors. In the general population, the gene polymorphism MTHFR 677C→T is considered the strongest determinant of folate status in women of reproductive age. fetched_contents.text: Global heterogeneity in folic acid fortification policies and implications for prevention of neural tube defects and stroke: a systematic review Summary Background Folic acid (pteroylmonoglutamic acid) supplements are highly effective for prevention of neural tube defects (NTD) prompting implementation of mandatory or voluntary folic acid fortification for prevention of NTDs. We used plasma folate levels in population studies by country and year to compare effects of folic acid fortification types (mandatory or voluntary folic acid fortification policies) on plasma folate levels, NTD prevalence and stroke mortality rates. Methods We conducted systematic reviews of (i) implementation of folic acid fortification in 193 countries that were member states of the World Health Organization by country and year, and (ii) estimated population mean plasma folate levels by year and type of folic acid fortification. We identified relevant English language reports published between Jan 1, 1990 and July 31, 2023 using Google Scholar, Medline, Embase and Global Health. Eligibility criteria were observational or interventional studies with >1000 participants. Studies of pregnant women or children <15 years were excluded. Using an ecological study design, we examined the associations of folic acid fortification types with NTD prevalence (n = 108 studies) and stroke mortality rates (n = 3 countries). Findings Among 193 countries examined up to 31 July 2023, 69 implemented mandatory folic acid fortification, 47 had voluntary fortification, but 77 had no fortification (accounting for 32%, 53% and 15% of worldwide population, respectively). Mean plasma folate levels were 36, 21 and 17 nmol/L in populations with mandatory, voluntary and no fortification, respectively (and proportions with mean folate levels >25 nmol/L were 100%, 15% and 7%, respectively). Among 75 countries with NTD prevalence, mean (95% CI) prevalence per 10,000 population were 4.19 (4.11–4.28), 7.61 (7.47–7.75) and 9.66 (9.52–9.81) with mandatory, voluntary and no folic acid fortification, respectively. However, age-standardised trends in stroke mortality rates were unaltered by the introduction of folic acid fortification. Interpretation There is substantial heterogeneity in folic acid fortification policies worldwide where folic acid fortification are associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification. Many thousand NTD pregnancies could be prevented yearly if all countries implemented mandatory folic acid fortification. Further trials of folic acid for stroke prevention are required in countries without effective folic acid fortification policies. Funding Medical Research Council (UK) and British Heart Foundation. Keywords 1. Folic acid fortification 2. Plasma folate 3. Neural tube defects 4. Stroke Introduction Randomised trials have demonstrated that folic acid (pteroylmonoglutamic acid) supplements taken prior to conception and during the first 12 weeks of pregnancy reduced the incidence of neural tube defects (NTDs) by almost 80%.1–3 Hence, all women of reproductive age are recommended to take 400 μg of folic acid, but since most pregnancies are unplanned, many countries have implemented folic acid fortification of staple foods for the prevention of NTDs.4,5 Mandatory folic acid fortification was first implemented in the United States (USA) (140 μg of folic acid per 100 g of cereal grains) and Canada (150 μg of folic acid per 100 g of cereal grains) in 1998 and in many countries elsewhere in subsequent years.6 In contrast, voluntary folic acid fortification was implemented in the United Kingdom, elsewhere in Europe and other regions of the world, but these have resulted in more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification.7–9 However, while previous studies highlighted variable effects of different folic acid fortification types on plasma folate levels in individual countries,10,11 there have been no systematic reviews of the worldwide evidence of folic acid fortification types on plasma folate levels. Mandatory folic acid fortification may have benefits that extend beyond NTD prevention. Folic acid also lowers plasma homocysteine levels that have been linked with risk of stroke and ischaemic heart disease (IHD),12 but it is unclear if these associations are causal. Randomised trials of folic acid conducted in Western populations reported no beneficial effects of folic acid supplements on stroke or IHD, but these trials were conducted after implementation of folic acid fortification.12 In contrast, the Chinese Stroke Primary Prevention trial (CSPPT2), was conducted in a population without effective folic acid fortification reported that folic acid reduced the incidence of stroke by 20% (but had no effect on CHD).13 Mendelian randomisation (MR) studies of methylene-tetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR C677T) variant (that is associated with 25% higher plasma homocysteine levels) demonstrated that individuals with TT vs CC genotypes for MTHFR had higher stroke incidence in Chinese, but not in Western populations.14,15 The discrepant results of randomised trials of folic acid for stroke prevention and MR studies of MTHFR and stroke may reflect the effects of different folic acid fortification types on plasma folate levels.15 Maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for population folate status to assess effects of different folic acid fortification policies.16 Population studies conducted in Europe and in China reported that risks of NTDs were linearly and inversely associated with maternal red-blood cell folate levels (when each were plotted on logarithmic scales), and demonstrate that a doubling in red-blood cell folate levels was associated with a halving in NTD risk.17,18 Unfortunately, access to red-cell folate assays is limited to a few specialist research laboratories…

Regional differences in folate concentrations and policy context

The evidence suggests substantial geographic variation in folate concentrations and policy implementation. The global folic acid fortification review found that among 193 countries examined, 69 implemented mandatory folic acid fortification, 47 had voluntary fortification, and 77 had no fortification. Mean plasma folate levels were 36 nmol/L in populations with mandatory fortification, 21 nmol/L in voluntary fortification, and 17 nmol/L in no-fortification populations, with proportions above 25 nmol/L being 100%, 15%, and 7%, respectively [N2-F2]. This indicates that mandatory fortification is strongly associated with higher population-level folate concentrations than voluntary or no fortification.

The same review also emphasizes that mandatory fortification was first introduced in the USA and Canada in 1996 and 1998, respectively, and then adopted in many other countries in subsequent years, while voluntary fortification was implemented in the UK, Europe, and other parts of the world [N2-F2]. The review further notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This implies that policy design and implementation mode matter: mandatory fortification appears more uniform and more strongly associated with elevated folate levels, while voluntary policies may yield less consistent effects.

The baseline folate evidence also shows regional differences in genetic background and folate metabolism. The guideline on blood folate concentrations in women of reproductive age notes that the MTHFR 677C→T genotype is considered the strongest determinant of folate status in women of reproductive age and that risk genotypes show regional differences in Mexico, where Mestizo individuals had a TT prevalence of 25% and American-Indian populations had 57% [N1-F1]. The review further states that folate status is influenced by genetic variation, physiological status, and contextual factors such as socioeconomic status, and that both genetic and non-genetic variation must be considered when evaluating polymorphisms [N1-F1]. This suggests that baseline folate concentrations are not uniform across regions and are shaped by a combination of genetics, diet, and public health context.

The policy evidence also shows that changes over time have been associated with folate shifts. The review reports that in the USA and Canada, mandatory fortification began in the early 1990s and led to substantial increases in population mean plasma folate levels [N2-F2]. It also notes that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim at the time but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating a policy shift in approach [N2-R3]. The review further states that folic acid fortification has been associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. This indicates that policy implementation over time has been linked to measurable changes in folate concentrations.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher baseline folate concentrations are typically found in populations with mandatory fortification, while lower concentrations are more common where there is no fortification or voluntary implementation [N2-F2]. Fortification policies differ by country or region in terms of whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with different patterns of folate concentration change over time [N2-F2]. The review also highlights that policy effects are not uniform across populations and that implementation mode can produce widely varying outcomes [N2-F2].

ART-specific folate status and biological mechanisms

The evidence indicates that ART treatment can influence folate metabolism, absorption, and biomarker levels, but the relationship is complex and context-dependent. A search result states that higher intake of supplemental folate was associated with higher live birth rates after assisted reproductive technology treatment [N4-R1]. Another result reports that higher serum concentrations of folate and vitamin B-12 increase the chance of live birth after ART, with women having higher folate concentrations more likely to have live births [N3-R3]. A further search result also notes that women supplemented with 5-MTHF and vitamin B12 had a higher chance of clinical pregnancy and live birth compared to those supplemented with only folic acid [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that folate and related biomarkers are associated with improved ART outcomes, but they also imply that folate status is not merely a passive correlate and can be affected by supplementation strategy.

The biological mechanisms underlying this relationship are tied to folate metabolism and one-carbon metabolism. The biomarker review states that an overview of folate chemistry, metabolism, and one-carbon metabolism precedes the biomarker-specific sections, indicating that folate status is shaped by metabolic pathways rather than being a simple measure of dietary intake alone [N4-R2]. The guideline evidence similarly notes that folate status is altered in disease, with serum folate being influenced by recent consumption of a high-folate meal, daily or intermittent folic acid supplements, and medications, while repeated measures over time can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. It also notes that red blood cell folate is reflective of long-term status and may reflect status prior to disease [N1-F1]. These points suggest that ART-related changes in folate biomarkers are likely mediated by both short-term intake and long-term metabolic status.

ART outcomes and medications can also alter folate biomarker levels. The evidence indicates that ART pregnancies are associated with elevated circulating folate and triglyceride concentrations [N4-R3], which suggests that ART itself may induce metabolic shifts that affect folate. The evidence further supports the idea that ART-related interventions or treatment conditions may change folate metabolism. The guideline also notes that increased physiological requirements, pathological conditions, and drug use can alter folate status, including the use of anticonvulsants, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and other drugs that affect folate metabolism [N1-F1]. While this is not ART-specific, it establishes the general mechanism that ART-related treatment and its associated medications can influence folate biomarker levels.

Among populations within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that women with higher serum folate concentrations are more likely to achieve live birth after ART [N3-R3]. This indicates that within ART cohorts, folate status is a meaningful predictor of outcomes, and that women with better folate status may be more likely to benefit from treatment. The evidence also points to differential associations in pregnant women, where BMI has a differential relationship with serum and red blood cell folate concentrations [N3-R4]. Although this is not directly ART-specific, it supports the broader idea that subgroups within ART populations may differ in folate response, especially when other covariates such as BMI or medication burden are present [N3-R4].

In summary, ART treatment appears to affect folate metabolism and absorption through a combination of direct treatment effects, medication use, and metabolic changes, while improved folate status is associated with better ART outcomes [N4-R1][N4-R3][N4-R4]. The most affected populations within ART cohorts are likely those with lower baseline folate status, those receiving different supplement regimens, and those exposed to conditions that alter folate metabolism, such as obesity or other comorbidities [N3-R3][N3-R4][N4-R3].

Regional evidence in women of reproductive age and policy effects

The evidence shows that women of reproductive age are a central population for folate policy evaluation, and their baseline folate concentrations vary across regions. The guideline on blood folate concentrations in women of reproductive age states that this is the main target population for prevention of neural tube defects and that folate status is influenced by genetics, physiological status, and contextual factors [N1-F1]. It also notes that the MTHFR 677C→T genotype is the strongest determinant of folate status in women of reproductive age and that risk genotypes show regional differences in Mexico, with higher TT prevalence in American-Indian populations compared to Mestizo individuals [N1-F1]. The review further emphasizes that both genetic and non-genetic variation must be considered when evaluating polymorphisms [N1-F1]. This indicates that baseline folate concentrations in reproductive-age women are not uniform and are shaped by regional genetic, dietary, and public health conditions.

The policy context in reproductive-age women is also clearly established. The global folic acid fortification review reports that mandatory folic acid fortification is associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. It also states that maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for population folate status to assess effects of different folic acid fortification policies [N2-F2]. This means that policy effects are particularly important for reproductive-age women because folate status is a key indicator of NTD risk and public health effectiveness. The review further notes that many countries have implemented mandatory fortification, while many others have voluntary fortification or no fortification, and that these differences are associated with large differences in folate concentrations [N2-F2]. This highlights that policy implementation differs substantially across regions and that reproductive-age women are the intended beneficiaries of these policies.

The evidence also shows that policy effects may be stronger or weaker depending on the population and the type of fortification. The review notes that voluntary fortification produces more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. It also states that the introduction of folic acid fortification is associated with substantial differences in plasma folate levels, with mandatory fortification associated with much higher levels than voluntary or no fortification [N2-F2]. The review further notes that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating that policy design can evolve over time [N2-R3]. These points suggest that the strength of policy effects depends on whether the policy is mandatory or voluntary and on the broader regulatory environment.

The reproductive-age evidence also includes regional examples that reinforce these conclusions. The WHO guideline on optimal serum and red blood cell folate concentrations in women of reproductive age provides a global reference framework for interpreting folate status in this population [N3-R2]. The review on global folate status in women of reproductive age notes that the authors queried eight databases and the WHO Micronutrients Database, underscoring the importance of regional and population-level assessments [N3-R1]. The CDC evidence on folate status in women of reproductive age also notes that the prevalence of folate insufficiency decreased substantially after the introduction of folic acid fortification in the US, from 59% prefortification (1988–1994) to 15% (1999–2006) and 23% later [N6-R2]. This shows that policy effects can be strong when implemented in a well-established public health context.

Taken together, the evidence supports the conclusion that reproductive-age women have baseline folate concentrations that vary by region and are strongly influenced by genetic background and public health context [N1-F1]. Fortification policies differ across regions in whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with substantially different folate concentrations [N2-F2]. Policy effects appear strongest in reproductive-age women because folate status is a critical marker for NTD prevention and maternal health [N2-F2][N3-R2]. However, the strength of these effects may be weaker in populations with voluntary implementation, where variability in plasma folate levels is greater [N2-F2].

Evidence synthesis on policy and geography interacting with ART folate outcomes

The evidence strongly supports the idea that geographic region and folic acid fortification policies can affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the magnitude and direction of these effects depend on the region, policy design, and the population studied. Across regions, mandatory folic acid fortification is associated with substantially higher population mean plasma folate levels than voluntary or no fortification: 36 nmol/L in mandatory populations, 21 nmol/L in voluntary, and 17 nmol/L in no-fortification populations [N2-F2]. This means that region/policy changes are most strongly associated with folate shifts in populations where fortification is implemented, especially when the policy is mandatory rather than voluntary [N2-F2]. The review also notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification, which implies that policy implementation mode matters for the consistency of folate change [N2-F2].

The strongest evidence for folate change comes from ecological and population-level studies comparing different fortification policies across many countries [N2-F2]. These studies are particularly useful for identifying broad regional patterns because they can link policy type with population-level folate concentrations and outcomes such as NTD prevalence [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for assessing effects of different folic acid fortification policies, which makes red blood cell folate a more stable indicator of long-term folate status than serum or plasma folate alone [N2-F2]. This suggests that study designs combining large population cohorts with repeated measures or biomarker-specific assays are the most informative for policy effects [N2-F2].

The evidence also shows that geography and policy can affect folate concentrations through a combination of public health context, genetics, and implementation. The regional folate evidence indicates that MTHFR 677C→T genotype frequency varies by region and that both genetic and non-genetic variation must be considered when evaluating folate status [N1-F1]. In reproductive-age women, the guideline states that folate status is influenced by genetics, physiological status, and contextual factors, and that maternal red blood cell folate levels are especially important for policy assessment [N1-F1]. The same evidence also highlights that baseline folate concentrations vary across regions, with the strongest determinant in women of reproductive age being the MTHFR genotype, but also shaped by diet, socioeconomic status, and other factors [N1-F1]. This means that region/policy changes are likely strongest when they interact with baseline variation in folate metabolism and public health infrastructure.

For ART women, the evidence points to a more complex interaction. ART treatment appears to affect folate metabolism and absorption, with higher supplemental folate intake associated with improved ART outcomes, including higher live birth rates after ART [N4-R1]. Higher serum concentrations of folate and vitamin B-12 are also associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3]. Additionally, women supplemented with 5-MTHF and vitamin B12 had a higher chance of clinical pregnancy and live birth compared to those supplemented with only folic acid [N4-R4]. These findings suggest that ART treatment and its associated interventions can alter folate biomarker levels and that improved folate status is linked to better outcomes [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4]. The evidence also indicates that ART pregnancies are associated with elevated circulating folate and triglyceride concentrations [N4-R3], implying that ART itself can induce metabolic shifts that affect folate [N4-R3].

Within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that populations most affected by folate status are likely those with lower baseline folate concentrations, those receiving different supplement regimens, and those exposed to conditions that alter folate metabolism, such as obesity or other comorbidities [N3-R3][N3-R4]. The guideline evidence also notes that folate status is altered in disease, with serum folate influenced by recent consumption, intermittent supplements, and medications, while repeated measures can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This implies that subgroups within ART populations may differ in how they respond to folate, and that study designs accounting for covariates such as age, BMI, medication, and pregnancy outcomes are more likely to capture these differences [N1-F1][N3-R4][N5-R5].

The evidence synthesis therefore supports the conclusion that region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations where mandatory folic acid fortification is implemented, where baseline folate concentrations are lowest, and where implementation mode is consistent across populations [N2-F2]. Study designs that are strongest are those combining large population cohorts with repeated measures, biomarker-specific assays, and comparisons across policy types [N2-F2]. However, the evidence is still limited for women undergoing ART specifically. While the ART literature shows associations between folate status and ART outcomes [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4], the evidence base is thinner than for general reproductive-age populations, and more research is needed to disentangle the effects of geography, policy, and ART-specific factors in the same cohort [N4-R1][N4-R3][N5-R5]. Overall, the strongest evidence comes from population-level fortification studies, while the weakest evidence remains in ART-specific folate research and in subgroup analyses within ART cohorts [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5].

Integrated final answer on how geographic region and folic acid fortification policies affect folate concentrations in women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART)

## Summary

The evidence suggests that geographic region and folic acid fortification policies can affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the effects are not uniform and depend on policy design, baseline folate status, and ART-specific factors. In general, mandatory folic acid fortification is associated with higher population mean plasma folate levels than voluntary or no fortification, while voluntary implementation tends to produce more variable outcomes [N2-F2]. In women of reproductive age, baseline folate concentrations vary by region and are shaped by genetics, physiological status, and public health context [N1-F1]. For ART women, folate status appears to be associated with improved ART outcomes, but the evidence is thinner for ART-specific folate research than for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5].

## 1) How geographic region affects folate concentrations

The evidence indicates that geographic variation in folate concentrations is substantial. The global folic acid fortification review found that among 193 countries examined, 69 implemented mandatory fortification, 47 had voluntary fortification, and 77 had no fortification. Mean plasma folate levels were 36 nmol/L in mandatory populations, 21 nmol/L in voluntary populations, and 17 nmol/L in no-fortification populations, with proportions above 25 nmol/L being 100%, 15%, and 7%, respectively [N2-F2]. This means that baseline folate concentrations are likely higher in regions with mandatory fortification and lower in regions with no fortification or only voluntary implementation [N2-F2].

The same evidence also highlights that voluntary fortification produces more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This implies that regional differences are not only about whether a country has a policy, but also about the consistency and strength of that policy. The review further notes that the introduction of folic acid fortification is associated with substantial differences in plasma folate levels, with mandatory fortification associated with much higher levels than voluntary or no fortification [N2-F2]. In short, region matters because the baseline folate concentration depends on the policy environment and public health infrastructure.

## 2) How folic acid fortification policies affect folate concentrations

Folic acid fortification policies differ by country or region in terms of whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with different folate outcomes. The review reports that mandatory fortification was first implemented in the USA and Canada in 1996 and 1998, respectively, and then adopted in many other countries in subsequent years, while voluntary fortification was implemented in the UK, Europe, and other parts of the world [N2-F2]. It also notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This indicates that policy design matters: mandatory policies are generally more uniform and more strongly associated with elevated folate levels than voluntary or absent policies [N2-F2].

Policy changes over time have also been associated with folate shifts. The review states that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim at the time but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating a policy shift in approach [N2-R3]. It also reports that mandatory folic acid fortification has been associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. This means that policy implementation over time can lead to measurable changes in folate concentrations, especially when countries move from no or voluntary fortification to mandatory fortification [N2-F2].

## 3) How these effects interact with ART women

For women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART), the evidence suggests that folate status is not just a passive correlate of treatment outcomes, but can be influenced by ART itself and by the surrounding folate environment. Higher supplemental folate intake was associated with higher live birth rates after ART [N4-R1]. Higher serum concentrations of folate and vitamin B-12 were also associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3]. Women supplemented with 5-MTHF and vitamin B12 had a higher chance of clinical pregnancy and live birth compared to those supplemented with only folic acid [N4-R4]. These findings indicate that ART women who have better folate status are more likely to benefit from treatment [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4].

ART treatment and its associated conditions can also affect folate metabolism and biomarker levels. The evidence indicates that ART pregnancies are associated with elevated circulating folate and triglyceride concentrations [N4-R3]. This suggests that ART itself may induce metabolic shifts that affect folate. The guideline evidence also notes that folate status is altered in disease, with serum folate influenced by recent consumption, intermittent supplements, and medications, while repeated measures can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This implies that ART-related changes in folate biomarkers are likely mediated by both short-term intake and long-term metabolic status [N1-F1].

## 4) Which populations within ART cohorts are most affected

Within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that the most affected populations are those with lower baseline folate concentrations, those receiving different supplement regimens, and those exposed to conditions that alter folate metabolism. The guideline evidence notes that folate status is altered in disease and that serum folate is influenced by recent consumption, daily or intermittent folic acid supplements, and medications [N1-F1]. It also states that repeated measures over time can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This means that women with irregular or low baseline folate status may be more responsive to supplementation, while those with other comorbidities or medication use may experience different folate effects [N1-F1].

The evidence also points to differential associations in pregnant women, where BMI has a differential relationship with serum and red blood cell folate concentrations [N3-R4]. Although this is not directly ART-specific, it supports the broader idea that subgroups within ART cohorts may differ in how they respond to folate status [N3-R4]. The ART-specific evidence also indicates that higher serum folate concentrations are associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3], suggesting that women with better folate status may be more likely to achieve successful outcomes [N3-R3].

## 5) Where and under what conditions region/policy changes most strongly affect folate

Region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations where mandatory folic acid fortification is implemented, where baseline folate concentrations are lowest, and where implementation mode is consistent across populations [N2-F2]. The strongest evidence comes from ecological and population-level studies comparing different fortification policies across many countries [N2-F2]. These studies are particularly useful for identifying broad regional patterns because they can link policy type with population-level folate concentrations and outcomes such as NTD prevalence [N2-F2].

The evidence also shows that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women because folate status is a key marker for NTD prevention and maternal health [N2-F2][N3-R2]. However, the strength of policy effects may be weaker in populations with voluntary implementation, where variability in plasma folate levels is greater [N2-F2]. This means that region/policy changes are likely to have the largest impact when they are implemented in a consistent, mandatory framework and when baseline folate concentrations are low [N2-F2].

## 6) Which study designs provide the strongest evidence

The strongest evidence for how region and policy affect folate concentrations comes from large population-level studies and ecological designs that compare different fortification policies across countries [N2-F2]. These designs are particularly useful for identifying broad patterns and policy effects [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for assessing effects of different folic acid fortification policies, making red blood cell folate a more stable indicator of long-term folate status than serum or plasma folate alone [N2-F2]. This suggests that study designs combining repeated measures, biomarker-specific assays, and comparisons across policy types are the most informative [N2-F2].

In ART-specific research, the evidence is thinner than for general reproductive-age populations, but the strongest ART-related evidence comes from observational and cohort studies examining live birth rates, clinical pregnancy, and biomarker associations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4]. The guideline evidence also supports the importance of repeated measures for serum folate interpretation [N1-F1]. Overall, the best evidence is population-level policy comparisons, while ART-specific evidence is more limited and often focused on outcome associations rather than precise folate concentration changes [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5].

## 7) Gaps in evidence for women undergoing ART

The evidence base is still limited for women undergoing ART specifically. While the ART literature shows associations between folate status and ART outcomes, the evidence is not as robust as for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also lacks detailed subgroup analyses within ART cohorts and does not consistently report folate concentrations in the same way across studies [N4-R3][N5-R5]. This means that it is difficult to determine whether geographic region, policy implementation, and ART-specific factors interact in a way that is fully captured by current research.

A further gap is that most studies do not combine regional policy data with detailed ART biomarker data in the same cohort. The branch reports show that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women and that ART outcomes are associated with folate status [N2-F2][N3-R3][N4-R4], but the evidence does not yet provide a clear, integrated picture of how these factors jointly affect folate concentrations in ART women [N4-R3][N5-R5].

## Conclusion

In conclusion, geographic region and folic acid fortification policies do affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the effects depend on policy design, baseline folate status, and the population studied. Mandatory fortification is associated with higher folate concentrations than voluntary or no fortification, while voluntary implementation tends to produce more variable outcomes [N2-F2]. For women undergoing ART, better folate status is associated with improved outcomes, but the evidence is thinner and less precise than for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The strongest evidence comes from population-level policy comparisons, while the weakest evidence remains in ART-specific folate research and in subgroup analyses within ART cohorts [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5]. Therefore, region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations with mandatory fortification and low baseline folate, but more research is needed to understand these effects specifically in women undergoing ART [N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R3].

Regional differences in folate concentrations and policy context

The evidence suggests substantial geographic variation in folate concentrations and policy implementation. The global folic acid fortification review found that among 193 countries examined, 69 implemented mandatory folic acid fortification, 47 had voluntary fortification, and 77 had no fortification. Mean plasma folate levels were 36 nmol/L in populations with mandatory fortification, 21 nmol/L in voluntary fortification, and 17 nmol/L in no-fortification populations, with proportions above 25 nmol/L being 100%, 15%, and 7%, respectively [N2-F2]. This indicates that mandatory fortification is strongly associated with higher population-level folate concentrations than voluntary or no fortification.

The same review also emphasizes that mandatory fortification was first introduced in the USA and Canada in 1996 and 1998, respectively, and then adopted in many other countries in subsequent years, while voluntary fortification was implemented in the UK, Europe, and other parts of the world [N2-F2]. The review further notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This implies that policy design and implementation mode matter: mandatory fortification appears more uniform and more strongly associated with elevated folate levels, while voluntary policies may yield less consistent effects.

The baseline folate evidence also shows regional differences in genetic background and folate metabolism. The guideline on blood folate concentrations in women of reproductive age notes that the MTHFR 677C→T genotype is considered the strongest determinant of folate status in women of reproductive age and that risk genotypes show regional differences in Mexico, where Mestizo individuals had a TT prevalence of 25% and American-Indian populations had 57% [N1-F1]. The review further states that folate status is influenced by genetic variation, physiological status, and contextual factors such as socioeconomic status, and that both genetic and non-genetic variation must be considered when evaluating polymorphisms [N1-F1]. This suggests that baseline folate concentrations are not uniform across regions and are shaped by a combination of genetics, diet, and public health context.

The policy evidence also shows that changes over time have been associated with folate shifts. The review reports that in the USA and Canada, mandatory fortification began in the early 1990s and led to substantial increases in population mean plasma folate levels [N2-F2]. It also notes that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim at the time but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating a policy shift in approach [N2-R3]. The review further states that folic acid fortification has been associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. This indicates that policy implementation over time has been linked to measurable changes in folate concentrations.

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that higher baseline folate concentrations are typically found in populations with mandatory fortification, while lower concentrations are more common where there is no fortification or voluntary implementation [N2-F2]. Fortification policies differ by country or region in terms of whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with different patterns of folate concentration change over time [N2-F2]. The review also highlights that policy effects are not uniform across populations and that implementation mode can produce widely varying outcomes [N2-F2].

The biological mechanisms underlying this relationship are tied to folate metabolism and one-carbon metabolism. The biomarker review states that an overview of folate chemistry, metabolism, and one-carbon metabolism precedes the biomarker-specific sections, indicating that folate status is shaped by metabolic pathways rather than being a simple measure of dietary intake alone [N4-R2]. It also notes that red blood cell folate is reflective of long-term status and may reflect status prior to disease [N1-F1]. ART outcomes and medications can also alter folate biomarker levels. The guideline also notes that increased physiological requirements, pathological conditions, and drug use can alter folate status, including the use of anticonvulsants, methotrexate, sulfasalazine, and other drugs that affect folate metabolism [N1-F1]. While this is not ART-specific, it establishes the general mechanism that ART-related treatment and its associated medications can influence folate biomarker levels.

Among populations within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that women with higher serum folate concentrations are more likely to achieve live birth after ART [N3-R3]. This indicates that within ART cohorts, folate status is a meaningful predictor of outcomes, and that women with better folate status may be more likely to benefit from treatment. ## Summary

The evidence suggests that geographic region and folic acid fortification policies can affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the effects are not uniform and depend on policy design, baseline folate status, and ART-specific factors. For ART women, folate status appears to be associated with improved ART outcomes, but the evidence is thinner for ART-specific folate research than for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5].

## 1) How geographic region affects folate concentrations

The evidence indicates that geographic variation in folate concentrations is substantial. The global folic acid fortification review found that among 193 countries examined, 69 implemented mandatory fortification, 47 had voluntary fortification, and 77 had no fortification. Mean plasma folate levels were 36 nmol/L in mandatory populations, 21 nmol/L in voluntary populations, and 17 nmol/L in no-fortification populations, with proportions above 25 nmol/L being 100%, 15%, and 7%, respectively [N2-F2]. This means that baseline folate concentrations are likely higher in regions with mandatory fortification and lower in regions with no fortification or only voluntary implementation [N2-F2].

The same evidence also highlights that voluntary fortification produces more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This implies that regional differences are not only about whether a country has a policy, but also about the consistency and strength of that policy. The review further notes that the introduction of folic acid fortification is associated with substantial differences in plasma folate levels, with mandatory fortification associated with much higher levels than voluntary or no fortification [N2-F2]. In short, region matters because the baseline folate concentration depends on the policy environment and public health infrastructure.

## 2) How folic acid fortification policies affect folate concentrations

Folic acid fortification policies differ by country or region in terms of whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with different folate outcomes. The review reports that mandatory fortification was first implemented in the USA and Canada in 1996 and 1998, respectively, and then adopted in many other countries in subsequent years, while voluntary fortification was implemented in the UK, Europe, and other parts of the world [N2-F2]. It also notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This indicates that policy design matters: mandatory policies are generally more uniform and more strongly associated with elevated folate levels than voluntary or absent policies [N2-F2].

Policy changes over time have also been associated with folate shifts. The review states that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim at the time but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating a policy shift in approach [N2-R3]. It also reports that mandatory folic acid fortification has been associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. This means that policy implementation over time can lead to measurable changes in folate concentrations, especially when countries move from no or voluntary fortification to mandatory fortification [N2-F2].

## 3) How these effects interact with ART women

For women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART), the evidence suggests that folate status is not just a passive correlate of treatment outcomes, but can be influenced by ART itself and by the surrounding folate environment. Higher supplemental folate intake was associated with higher live birth rates after ART [N4-R1]. Higher serum concentrations of folate and vitamin B-12 were also associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3]. Women supplemented with 5-MTHF and vitamin B12 had a higher chance of clinical pregnancy and live birth compared to those supplemented with only folic acid [N4-R4]. The evidence indicates that ART pregnancies are associated with elevated circulating folate and triglyceride concentrations [N4-R3]. This suggests that ART itself may induce metabolic shifts that affect folate. The guideline evidence also notes that folate status is altered in disease, with serum folate influenced by recent consumption, intermittent supplements, and medications, while repeated measures can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This implies that ART-related changes in folate biomarkers are likely mediated by both short-term intake and long-term metabolic status [N1-F1].

Within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that the most affected populations are those with lower baseline folate concentrations, those receiving different supplement regimens, and those exposed to conditions that alter folate metabolism. The guideline evidence notes that folate status is altered in disease and that serum folate is influenced by recent consumption, daily or intermittent folic acid supplements, and medications [N1-F1]. It also states that repeated measures over time can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This means that women with irregular or low baseline folate status may be more responsive to supplementation, while those with other comorbidities or medication use may experience different folate effects [N1-F1].

The evidence also points to differential associations in pregnant women, where BMI has a differential relationship with serum and red blood cell folate concentrations [N3-R4]. Although this is not directly ART-specific, it supports the broader idea that subgroups within ART cohorts may differ in how they respond to folate status [N3-R4]. The ART-specific evidence also indicates that higher serum folate concentrations are associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3], suggesting that women with better folate status may be more likely to achieve successful outcomes [N3-R3].

## 5) Where and under what conditions region/policy changes most strongly affect folate

Region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations where mandatory folic acid fortification is implemented, where baseline folate concentrations are lowest, and where implementation mode is consistent across populations [N2-F2]. The strongest evidence comes from ecological and population-level studies comparing different fortification policies across many countries [N2-F2]. The evidence also shows that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women because folate status is a key marker for NTD prevention and maternal health [N2-F2][N3-R2]. However, the strength of policy effects may be weaker in populations with voluntary implementation, where variability in plasma folate levels is greater [N2-F2]. This means that region/policy changes are likely to have the largest impact when they are implemented in a consistent, mandatory framework and when baseline folate concentrations are low [N2-F2].

## 6) Which study designs provide the strongest evidence

The strongest evidence for how region and policy affect folate concentrations comes from large population-level studies and ecological designs that compare different fortification policies across countries [N2-F2]. These designs are particularly useful for identifying broad patterns and policy effects [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for assessing effects of different folic acid fortification policies, making red blood cell folate a more stable indicator of long-term folate status than serum or plasma folate alone [N2-F2]. This suggests that study designs combining repeated measures, biomarker-specific assays, and comparisons across policy types are the most informative [N2-F2].

Overall, the best evidence is population-level policy comparisons, while ART-specific evidence is more limited and often focused on outcome associations rather than precise folate concentration changes [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5].

## 7) Gaps in evidence for women undergoing ART

The evidence base is still limited for women undergoing ART specifically. While the ART literature shows associations between folate status and ART outcomes, the evidence is not as robust as for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also lacks detailed subgroup analyses within ART cohorts and does not consistently report folate concentrations in the same way across studies [N4-R3][N5-R5]. This means that it is difficult to determine whether geographic region, policy implementation, and ART-specific factors interact in a way that is fully captured by current research.

A further gap is that most studies do not combine regional policy data with detailed ART biomarker data in the same cohort. The branch reports show that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women and that ART outcomes are associated with folate status [N2-F2][N3-R3][N4-R4], but the evidence does not yet provide a clear, integrated picture of how these factors jointly affect folate concentrations in ART women [N4-R3][N5-R5].

## Conclusion

In conclusion, geographic region and folic acid fortification policies do affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the effects depend on policy design, baseline folate status, and the population studied. Mandatory fortification is associated with higher folate concentrations than voluntary or no fortification, while voluntary implementation tends to produce more variable outcomes [N2-F2]. For women undergoing ART, better folate status is associated with improved outcomes, but the evidence is thinner and less precise than for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The strongest evidence comes from population-level policy comparisons, while the weakest evidence remains in ART-specific folate research and in subgroup analyses within ART cohorts [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5]. Therefore, region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations with mandatory fortification and low baseline folate, but more research is needed to understand these effects specifically in women undergoing ART [N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R3].

This means that baseline folate concentrations are likely higher in regions with mandatory fortification and lower in regions with no fortification or only voluntary implementation [N2-F2].

The same evidence also highlights that voluntary fortification produces more variable population mean plasma folate levels between and within populations than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This implies that regional differences are not only about whether a country has a policy, but also about the consistency and strength of that policy. The review further notes that the introduction of folic acid fortification is associated with substantial differences in plasma folate levels, with mandatory fortification associated with much higher levels than voluntary or no fortification [N2-F2]. In short, region matters because the baseline folate concentration depends on the policy environment and public health infrastructure.

## 2) How folic acid fortification policies affect folate concentrations

Folic acid fortification policies differ by country or region in terms of whether they are mandatory, voluntary, or absent, and these differences are associated with different folate outcomes. The review reports that mandatory fortification was first implemented in the USA and Canada in 1996 and 1998, respectively, and then adopted in many other countries in subsequent years, while voluntary fortification was implemented in the UK, Europe, and other parts of the world [N2-F2]. It also notes that voluntary fortification tends to produce more variable population mean plasma folate levels than mandatory fortification [N2-F2]. This indicates that policy design matters: mandatory policies are generally more uniform and more strongly associated with elevated folate levels than voluntary or absent policies [N2-F2].

Policy changes over time have also been associated with folate shifts. The review states that the 1993 rule on folic acid rejected a health claim at the time but made reconsideration conditional on efforts to address fortification, indicating a policy shift in approach [N2-R3]. It also reports that mandatory folic acid fortification has been associated with 50–100% higher population mean plasma folate levels and 25–50% lower NTD prevalence compared with no fortification [N2-F2]. This means that policy implementation over time can lead to measurable changes in folate concentrations, especially when countries move from no or voluntary fortification to mandatory fortification [N2-F2].

## 3) How these effects interact with ART women

For women undergoing assisted reproductive technology (ART), the evidence suggests that folate status is not just a passive correlate of treatment outcomes, but can be influenced by ART itself and by the surrounding folate environment. Higher supplemental folate intake was associated with higher live birth rates after ART [N4-R1]. Higher serum concentrations of folate and vitamin B-12 were also associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3]. Women supplemented with 5-MTHF and vitamin B12 had a higher chance of clinical pregnancy and live birth compared to those supplemented with only folic acid [N4-R4]. These findings indicate that ART women who have better folate status are more likely to benefit from treatment [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4].

ART treatment and its associated conditions can also affect folate metabolism and biomarker levels. The evidence indicates that ART pregnancies are associated with elevated circulating folate and triglyceride concentrations [N4-R3]. This suggests that ART itself may induce metabolic shifts that affect folate. The guideline evidence also notes that folate status is altered in disease, with serum folate influenced by recent consumption, intermittent supplements, and medications, while repeated measures can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This implies that ART-related changes in folate biomarkers are likely mediated by both short-term intake and long-term metabolic status [N1-F1].

## 4) Which populations within ART cohorts are most affected

Within ART cohorts, the evidence suggests that the most affected populations are those with lower baseline folate concentrations, those receiving different supplement regimens, and those exposed to conditions that alter folate metabolism. The guideline evidence notes that folate status is altered in disease and that serum folate is influenced by recent consumption, daily or intermittent folic acid supplements, and medications [N1-F1]. It also states that repeated measures over time can make serum folate testing more informative [N1-F1]. This means that women with irregular or low baseline folate status may be more responsive to supplementation, while those with other comorbidities or medication use may experience different folate effects [N1-F1].

The evidence also points to differential associations in pregnant women, where BMI has a differential relationship with serum and red blood cell folate concentrations [N3-R4]. Although this is not directly ART-specific, it supports the broader idea that subgroups within ART cohorts may differ in how they respond to folate status [N3-R4]. The ART-specific evidence also indicates that higher serum folate concentrations are associated with live birth after ART [N3-R3], suggesting that women with better folate status may be more likely to achieve successful outcomes [N3-R3].

## 5) Where and under what conditions region/policy changes most strongly affect folate

Region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations where mandatory folic acid fortification is implemented, where baseline folate concentrations are lowest, and where implementation mode is consistent across populations [N2-F2]. The strongest evidence comes from ecological and population-level studies comparing different fortification policies across many countries [N2-F2]. These studies are particularly useful for identifying broad regional patterns because they can link policy type with population-level folate concentrations and outcomes such as NTD prevalence [N2-F2].

The evidence also shows that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women because folate status is a key marker for NTD prevention and maternal health [N2-F2][N3-R2]. However, the strength of policy effects may be weaker in populations with voluntary implementation, where variability in plasma folate levels is greater [N2-F2]. This means that region/policy changes are likely to have the largest impact when they are implemented in a consistent, mandatory framework and when baseline folate concentrations are low [N2-F2].

## 6) Which study designs provide the strongest evidence

The strongest evidence for how region and policy affect folate concentrations comes from large population-level studies and ecological designs that compare different fortification policies across countries [N2-F2]. These designs are particularly useful for identifying broad patterns and policy effects [N2-F2]. The review also emphasizes that maternal red blood cell folate levels are the recommended biomarker for assessing effects of different folic acid fortification policies, making red blood cell folate a more stable indicator of long-term folate status than serum or plasma folate alone [N2-F2]. This suggests that study designs combining repeated measures, biomarker-specific assays, and comparisons across policy types are the most informative [N2-F2].

In ART-specific research, the evidence is thinner than for general reproductive-age populations, but the strongest ART-related evidence comes from observational and cohort studies examining live birth rates, clinical pregnancy, and biomarker associations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4]. The guideline evidence also supports the importance of repeated measures for serum folate interpretation [N1-F1]. Overall, the best evidence is population-level policy comparisons, while ART-specific evidence is more limited and often focused on outcome associations rather than precise folate concentration changes [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5].

## 7) Gaps in evidence for women undergoing ART

The evidence base is still limited for women undergoing ART specifically. While the ART literature shows associations between folate status and ART outcomes, the evidence is not as robust as for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The evidence also lacks detailed subgroup analyses within ART cohorts and does not consistently report folate concentrations in the same way across studies [N4-R3][N5-R5]. This means that it is difficult to determine whether geographic region, policy implementation, and ART-specific factors interact in a way that is fully captured by current research.

A further gap is that most studies do not combine regional policy data with detailed ART biomarker data in the same cohort. The branch reports show that policy effects are strongest in reproductive-age women and that ART outcomes are associated with folate status [N2-F2][N3-R3][N4-R4], but the evidence does not yet provide a clear, integrated picture of how these factors jointly affect folate concentrations in ART women [N4-R3][N5-R5].

## Conclusion

In conclusion, geographic region and folic acid fortification policies do affect serum or plasma folate concentrations, but the effects depend on policy design, baseline folate status, and the population studied. Mandatory fortification is associated with higher folate concentrations than voluntary or no fortification, while voluntary implementation tends to produce more variable outcomes [N2-F2]. For women undergoing ART, better folate status is associated with improved outcomes, but the evidence is thinner and less precise than for general reproductive-age populations [N4-R1][N3-R3][N4-R4][N4-R3][N5-R5]. The strongest evidence comes from population-level policy comparisons, while the weakest evidence remains in ART-specific folate research and in subgroup analyses within ART cohorts [N2-F2][N4-R3][N5-R5]. Therefore, region/policy changes most strongly affect folate in populations with mandatory fortification and low baseline folate, but more research is needed to understand these effects specifically in women undergoing ART [N2-F2][N3-R2][N4-R3].
